reason: Egypt's main cargo artery: grain, sugar and Red Sea goods moved by Nile boats between the Delta, Cairo (Bulaq/Fustat) and Upper Egypt throughout the period.

sea_head.evidence: Sea craft crossed the Rosetta bar only as far as Rosetta, where cargo for Cairo was shifted to river boats.

river_head.evidence: The First Cataract at Aswan was the normal end of Egyptian river traffic and the trans-shipment point for Nubia.

head.evidence: Damietta at the eastern mouth was the sea port for Levant trade, linked to Cairo by the Damietta branch.

branches.river: Alexandria canal (Khalij al-Iskandariyya, later Mahmudiyya canal)

head.evidence: A canal from the Rosetta branch near Fuwa carried Nile boats to Alexandria; re-dug in 1311 and rebuilt as the Mahmudiyya canal in 1820.

period_note: Whole Egyptian Nile Rosetta/Damietta -> Cairo -> Qus/Qena -> Aswan. Qus (tag qus) was the main Upper Egyptian port for the Red Sea route in the 13th-14th c. Nubian reach above Aswan excluded: Second-Sixth Cataracts break it into short local stretches. Alexandria canal was flood-season only before 1820 (confidence medium for the canal).

reason: Tidal estuary that let Indian Ocean ships reach Basra, the Gulf port of Iraq.

sea_head.evidence: Basra was the head of sea-going navigation on the Shatt al-Arab and Iraq's port for Gulf and Indian trade.

period_note: Mouth locations abadan / zuwayr. River traffic continues up the Tigris (see Tigris); confluence at al-Qurna (no tag; nearest river location al_madar or basra).

reason: Boats regularly carried merchants and goods between Basra and Baghdad (e.g. Ralph Fitch 1583), the main river link of Iraq.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships stopped at Basra; cargo continued up the Tigris by river boat.

river_head.evidence: Baghdad was the upstream terminus of regular boat traffic from Basra; above it the river was mostly run downstream by kelek rafts from Mosul.

period_note: Reach Basra -> Qurna -> Wasit/Kut -> Baghdad. Mosul-Baghdad kelek (raft) traffic excluded as downstream-only. Steamers ran Basra-Baghdad from the 1830s-60s (Lynch).

reason: Excluded: 16th-c. merchants floated down from Birecik to Falluja in boats that were sold at the end, so traffic was essentially downstream-only, and the lower river ran into the Bata'ih marshes.
period_note: If wanted as a borderline case: Birecik (birecik) -> Raqqa (raqqa) -> Anah (anah) -> Hit (hit) -> Falluja (al_anbar), documented by Federici, Rauwolf and Fitch; upstream the boats were towed only with great difficulty. Chesney's 1836 steamer expedition proved it navigable but no regular service followed.

reason: Excluded: commercial navigation to Ahvaz opened only in 1888, and medieval Ahvaz trade had long declined by 1337.
period_note: Would be Muhammerah (muhammerah) -> Ahvaz (ahvaz), rapids at Ahvaz, small boats above to Shushtar (shushtar).

reason: Excluded: no well-attested regular cargo boat traffic in 1300-1600; the river was crossed by ferries and flows into the landlocked Aral Sea.
period_note: Medieval geographers mention boats between Termez and Khwarazm and Russia ran an Aral flotilla from the 1850s, both outside the focus period.

reason: Excluded: no regular cargo navigation in the period; ends in the Aral Sea.
Excluded: lower Kura traffic was mainly fishery boats at Salyan; steamer navigation up to Mingachevir is 19th century.
Large canoes and barges carried grain, salt and gold between Djenne, Timbuktu's port Kabara and Gao, the core trade axis of Mali and Songhai.

river_head.evidence: Segou/Sansanding was the upstream trade port of the middle Niger canoe network (Mungo Park saw heavy traffic there in 1796).

head.evidence: Djenne on the Bani floodplain shipped goods by boat down to Timbuktu.

period_note: lower_end: gao. Disconnected from the sea by the Ansongo-Labbezanga rapids below Gao and the Bussa rapids further down. Timbuktu itself (tag timbuktu, has_river False) is served by its port Kabara (tag kabara). High-water navigation also reaches Koulikoro (koulikoro); Sotuba rapids at Bamako above that.

reason: Large trade canoes of Aboh, Onitsha and the Igala carried palm oil, yams, salt and slaves between the Delta and the Niger-Benue confluence.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going ships traded at the Delta ports and did not ascend the river before Laird's steamers of 1832.

river_head.evidence: Canoe trade from the Delta through Onitsha and Idah reached the confluence; rapids near Jebba and Bussa end navigation above.

period_note: Evidence is mostly 18th-19th c. (Lander 1830, Laird 1832); pre-1600 volume uncertain, hence low confidence. Intermediate: onitsha, idah. Benue excluded (flood-season only).

reason: European barques and local boats sailed each high-water season from Saint-Louis to Galam carrying gum, grain and slaves (17th-19th c.).

sea_head.evidence: Saint-Louis at the mouth was the head of sea-going traffic; ships had to cross a dangerous bar.

river_head.evidence: The Galam trading posts near Bakel were the upriver terminus, reached only in the July-October flood.

period_note: Seasonal but substantial; intermediate podor, matam. Felou falls above Kayes (tag kayes) mark the absolute limit; Medine 1855 extends the head to Kayes only in the late 19th c.

reason: Portuguese and English ships and sloops sailed far up the Gambia to trade at Kassan and the Wuli markets from the 15th century on.

sea_head.evidence: Sea-going vessels regularly ascended to the Kassan-Kuntaur reach (no Kassan tag; wassu is the nearest river location).

river_head.evidence: Boats continued to the Wuli markets below Barrakunda Falls, the limit reached by Richard Jobson in 1620.

period_note: Mouth location: tag gambia (Banjul/James Island area; juffure and albreda have has_river False). Barrakunda Falls lie just above the head.

reason: Excluded: only canoe salt trade from Ada upriver, broken by the Senchi rapids.
Excluded: navigable only in the flood season and used by steamers only from the 1850s.
Excluded: in 1300-1600 sea ships traded only at the mouth (Mpinda/Soyo), Livingstone Falls block the river below Pool Malebo, and the big Bobangi canoe trade above the Pool is 18th-19th c.

reason: The Portuguese supply route from the coast to their forts at Muxima, Massangano and Cambambe ran by boat on the Kwanza (late 16th-17th c.).

sea_head.evidence: Sea ships stayed at Luanda; small craft entered the Kwanza bar (Calumbo is the nearest tagged river location near the mouth).

river_head.evidence: The falls at Cambambe ended boat traffic; Massangano (1583) and Cambambe were the upriver Portuguese posts.

period_note: Intermediate muxima (Muxima 1599). The Massangano tag in the file is the Zambezi one (lower_mazowe_province), do not use it for the Kwanza.

reason: Swahili and then Portuguese boats carried cloth, beads and gold/ivory between the coast and the inland markets of Sena and Tete from the 16th century.

sea_head.evidence: Sea ships anchored at the Zambezi mouths (Cuama) and cargo went up in river boats.

river_head.evidence: Tete was the upstream trade post; the Cahora Bassa rapids just above stopped boats.

head.evidence: Quelimane at the mouth of the Qua Qua became the main sea port for the Zambezi, connected in flood season through the Mazaro channel.

period_note: Reach cuama/chindre -> chupanga -> sena -> Lupata gorge (navigable) -> tete. Shire excluded (Murchison cataracts, 19th-c. traffic only). Quelimane branch is seasonal (medium confidence).

reason: Excluded: navigation to Chiromo is 19th-century steamer traffic, blocked above by the Murchison cataracts.
